name: Nicarchus
bio: Nicarchus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century AD.
This archive carries the 5 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book V: 38, 39, 40; Book VI: 31, 285).

poems.title: Book V, 38
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A fine and largely built woman attracts me, Similus, whether she be in her prime, or elderly. If she be young she will clasp me, if she be old and wrinkled, me fellabit.

poems.title: Book V, 39
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Must I not die? What care I if I go to Hades with gouty legs or in training for a race? I shall have many to carry me; so let me become lame, if I wish. As far as that goes, as you see, I am quite easy, and never miss a banquet.

poems.title: Book V, 40
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Don’t listen to your mother, Philumena; for once I am off and out of the town, pay no attention to those who make fun of us, but give them tit for tat, and try to be more successful than I was. Leave no stone unturned, make your own living, and write and tell me what pleasances you have visited. Try and behave with propriety. If you have anything over, pay the rent and get a coat for me. If you get with child, bring it to the birth, I entreat you. Don’t be troubled about that: when it grows up it will find out who its father was.

poems.title: Book VI, 31
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.note: Paton marks the attribution with a query.
poems.text: I nave offered this as a common gift to Pan the goattreader, to Dionysus the giver of good fruit, and to Demeter the Earth-goddess, and I beg from them fine flocks, good wine and to gather good grain from the ears.

poems.title: Book VI, 285
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.note: Paton marks the attribution with a query.
poems.text: Nicarete, who formerly was in the service of Athene’s shuttle, and stretched out many a warp on the loom, made in honour of Cypris a bonfire in front of her house of her work-basket and bobbins and her other gear, crying, “Away with ye, starving work of wretched women, that have power to waste away the bloom of youth.” Instead the girl chose garlands and the lyre, and a gay life spent in revel and festivity. “Cypris,” she said, “I will pay thee tithe of all my gains. Give me work and take from it thy due.”

poems.title: Book VII, 159
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Orpheus won the highest prize among mortals by his harp, Nestor by the skill of his sweet-phrased tongue, divine Homer, the learned in lore, by the art of his verse, but Telephanes, whose tomb this is, by the flute.
